title: CrabRAG: Why Automated Assistants Need Graph Memory, Not More Tokens — Stephen Chin, Neo4j

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core subject is GraphRAG architecture, comparing vector store vs graph store retrieval for multi-hop queries with live demos of retrieval quality differences. The talk addresses agent memory and retrieval architecture generally, with security-themed demos on finding exposed ports and end-of-life software in a home lab. A home lab prototype demo validates the approach, followed by discussion of enterprise-scale production deployment where data exceeds context window limits. Requires familiarity with agent memory, vector databases, and embeddings, but explicitly lowers the barrier by noting Claude can write Cypher queries. Conference talk with live demonstrations, code walkthroughs, and resource announcements. Claims are substantiated by live side-by-side demos comparing vector vs graph agents on identical data with concrete security findings.

summary: Stephen Chin from Neo4j frames the talk around Crab D, a crustacean-themed agent mascot whose core problem is bad memory. Most agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Goose) store memory as markdown files on disk—solved.md, daily memory files, tool files, skills files—loading everything into context each round in hopes something is relevant. Chin's average agents consume over 100k tokens per round. This works at small scale with high-quality models but breaks at large scale. Goose, part of the Agentic AI Foundation backed by Anthropic, treats memory as an MCP server with 70+ extensions but still stores memories as plain files. Vector databases (PGVector, LanceDB) improve retrieval via similarity search, but similarity in vector space is not the same as actual relationships, leading to hallucinations and failure on complex multi-hop queries. Graphs solve this by storing entities as nodes and relationships as edges, with properties and embeddings on top. The recommended architecture uses vector search to find seed nodes, then graph traversal to pull nearest neighbors ranked by relatedness. Graphs are precise, explainable, and auditable. Claude writes Cypher better than Chin and can build entity extractors, lowering the barrier to graph adoption. The live demo uses a home lab digital twin built on Cogney with a Neo4j backend, with two environments from the same markdown source: one vector store and one graph store. When asked to find exposed end-of-life software, the vector agent said it could not find specific details, while the graph agent traced the connections and flagged the daughter's Minecraft server (Tinkster Lands) running Debian 8 Jessie. When asked to find management ports exposed to the WAN (0.0.0.0), the vector agent told Chin to check the pfSense configuration himself, while the graph agent found HAProxy and OpenVPN exposed to the internet, traversing from the router node directly to all related results. Chin patched all discovered security holes after the demo. For large-scale enterprise use—data centers, financial services, large customer record sets—graph memory is essential because data won't fit in a 1-million-token context window. Chin announces GraphRAG: The Definitive Guide, co-authored with Michael Hunger and Jesús Barrasa, and highlights Neo4j's free Graph Academy online training courses on agent memory, context graphs, and GraphRAG.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Meet Crab D and the agent memory problem
sections.summary: Chin introduces Crab D, a personal assistant agent mascot who forgets everything daily because his memory file flips. Agents wake up on new memory files and remember nothing from previous days. They have many tools but pick the wrong ones, and are forgetful about people and tasks.

sections.title: Why markdown memory wastes tokens
sections.summary: OpenClaw structures memory as markdown files (solved.md, memory files, tool files, daily files). Markdown is easy to read but wastes tokens; Chin's agents load 100k+ tokens per round loading everything hoping something is useful. Works at small scale, breaks at large scale. He announces a home lab digital twin demo.

sections.title: Skills are just markdown too
sections.summary: Hermes agent has a better memory system that reflects and adds new skills after tasks. But skills are still markdown files. Agents sometimes load the wrong skill. A Neo4j colleague has an arxiv paper on graph for skills. Chin suggests we can do better.

sections.title: Goose: memory as an MCP server
sections.summary: Goose is part of the Agentic AI Foundation, backed by Anthropic, with 70+ MCP extensions. It treats memory as an MCP server with remember, retrieve, and forget commands. But memories are still plain files on disk—same fundamental problem. Picking the wrong tool or having too many memories encumbers the agent.

sections.title: Vector databases and why similarity is not a relationship
sections.summary: Vector databases store embeddings and do similarity search. OpenClaw includes PGVector; LanceDB is another option. But similarity in vector space is not the same as actual relationships, causing hallucinations. Multi-hop reasoning chains don't work on similarity searches and are expensive on relational databases. Things look similar but aren't the same.

sections.title: Enter graphs: precise, explainable, auditable
sections.summary: Graphs use nodes, edges, and properties, and can store embeddings. The demo architecture seeds traversal with vector search results, then pulls nearest neighbors ranked by relatedness. Graphs give precise, explainable, and auditable answers. Developers can introspect graphs, reduce duplicate nodes, and converge on good answers.

sections.title: You do not need to be a graph expert, Claude writes Cypher
sections.summary: Claude can write Cypher better than Chin and can build entity extractors. Developers just need a basic model of what they want to accomplish. The plan: have Claude write each action into the graph, traverse rather than re-read, and retrieve results in a fresh session.

sections.title: The demo: a home lab digital twin, vector versus graph
sections.summary: Chin built a digital twin of his home lab as a graph over the past two weeks. Two separate environments from the same original markdown files: one vector database store (test A) and one graph store (test B) built on Cogney with Neo4j backend. The home lab has Proxmox servers on a separate segmented VLAN. The demo is about to begin with five queued questions.

sections.title: Live: finding end of life software on the network
sections.summary: Chin opens the CrabRAG cockpit and asks both agents to find exposed end-of-life software. The vector agent says it could not find specific details. The graph agent fires Cypher queries, traverses from seed nodes (blue) through one-hop nodes (gray) to winning context nodes (green), and identifies the daughter's Minecraft server Tinkster Lands running Debian 8 Jessie with precise, actionable information.

sections.title: Live: finding exposed management ports
sections.summary: Chin asks both agents to find management ports exposed to 0.0.0.0. The vector agent tells him to check the pfSense configuration himself. The graph agent finds HAProxy and OpenVPN exposed to the WAN by locating the pfSense router node and traversing directly to all related results, producing a very precise answer with a different graph shape from the previous query.

sections.title: Why large scale needs graph memory
sections.summary: Chin patched all discovered security holes after the demo. For enterprise-scale data centers, financial services with large customer record sets, or any scenario where data won't fit in a 1-million-token context window, markdown memory is insufficient. Graph memory is essential at large scale.

sections.title: Resources: the GraphRAG book and GraphAcademy
sections.summary: Chin announces GraphRAG: The Definitive Guide, co-authored with Michael Hunger and Jesús Barrasa, covering GraphRAG, memory, agents, and industry vertical use cases, available on early release. He also highlights Neo4j Graph Academy, free online training at dev.neo4j.com/ga-rag, with courses on agent memory, context graphs, and GraphRAG. Chin invites attendees to stay for the graph track and visit the Neo4j booth.
